Yes but not on our current path. Evolution by natural selection is ultimately a measure of reproductive success meaning that for evolution to occur some genes must be passed down more than others. What this looks like is individuals with more beneficial genes (cigarette smoke resistance) are more likely to survive and pass on these genes to offspring than those that don't have the genes. For this to work, there would first have to be a smoking resistance gene of sorts (maybe there is maybe there isn't, idk), and those with the gene must be more likely to survive and have children than those that don't have the gene. As we all know hardly any smoker dies before childbearing years, so there is no selection of genes and therefore no evolution. Sorry for the wall of text, but too often people throw around the word evolution without explaining the mechanism behind it leading to confusion and somewhat understandable denial.

The answer is "technically yes, but only in a really long time frame and probably not very well."

Digesting lactose is a specific thing - once you get the metabolic pathway to do it, you're done.

In contrast, resistance to smoke is a broad thing - many different stresses and toxins need to be guarded against before you see a beneficial effect.
